documents.title: It Doesn't Pay to Be Female or Black (Washington Post / Guild clipping)
documents.subject: Pay discrimination at The Washington Post: salary gaps by sex and race across job categories, comparing 1982 and 1986 figures
documents.date: approx 1986 (compares 1982 vs 1986 data); handwritten annotation 'DATE?' on page
documents.notes: Printed clipping/newsletter page, likely Guild-produced, headlined 'At The Washington Post — It Doesn't Pay to Be Female or Black'. Includes partial bar chart 'REPORTERS: HOW OTHER SALARIES COMPARE TO WHITE MALE AVERAGE SALARIES, 1982 & 1986' at bottom. Handwritten 'DATE?' in upper right suggests it was collected as evidence without a confirmed date.

pages.transcript:
[handwritten, top right] DATE?

At The Washington Post
It Doesn't Pay to Be Female or Black

Five years ago, the Washington Post company settled a sex discrimination case brought against it by the Guild by agreeing to hire more women. The company reported to the federal government recently that it has more than met its hiring goals in every category, and in every department.

What it did not tell the government is that it is paying those women, as well as its black male employees, less than it pays white men.

In the best paying jobs and in many of the largest job categories, the Washington Post pays white men significantly higher salaries on average than white women or blacks doing the same jobs. This is pay discrimination.

Patterns of pay discrimination that existed four years ago not only persist, but in some cases have worsened with the gap between the salaries of white males and others growing wider.

In the case of reporters — the largest single job category covered by the contract — the average salary for white men is $988.68. Black men average $920.46; white women reporters average $859.37, and black women reporters average salaries of $791.33.

Although in some jobs the gap has narrowed between the salaries of white males and black males, women, especially black women, have been left further and further behind.

In the case of reporters, for instance, white women reporters were paid 11.2 percent less on average than their white male colleagues in 1982; now they are paid 13.1 percent less. In 1982, black female reporters were paid 15.8 percent less than their white male counterparts. Four years later, they are paid 20 percent less than their white male co-workers. In 1982, black men were paid 14.7 percent below on average than white male reporters; in 1986, they have narrowed the gap and are paid 7 percent less.

In 1982, in the category of assistant editors, assignment editors and makeup editors, white women were paid 5.5 percent less well than white males in those jobs. That gap has grown to 8.6 percent in 1986. In 1982, all blacks (9 of them) were paid 4.9 percent less than their white male colleagues. Now there are 10 blacks in this category, and nothing has changed: They make 4.8 percent less than their white male counterparts.

Those two categories alone account for 277 — or about a quarter — of the fulltime employes covered by the current Guild contract.

There have been some improvements in the past for years, however. In outside advertising sales, white males average $809.21 in weekly salary. White females average $766.18. Average weekly pay for all blacks is $784.24. (To break down the data for the nine blacks in the department by sex might indicate individual salaries.)

Disparities in pay were worse in that department in 1982. Then white female employes received salaries 18 percent lower than the salaries of their white male colleagues. Now the gap is only 5.3 percent. Then blacks received salaries 4.3 percent lower than their white male colleagues. Now the gap is 3.1 percent.

In some departments dominated by women or by blacks (generally the lower paying jobs), white males often are not the best paid workers. In telephone sales, for instance, black women command the highest salaries.

[chart, partially cut off at bottom of page] REPORTERS — HOW OTHER SALARIES COMPARE TO WHITE MALE AVERAGE SALARIES, 1982 & 1986. Bars shown: WHITE FEMALE -11.2% (1982) and -13.1% (1986); BLACK MALE -14.7% and -7%; BLACK FEMALE -15.8% (1982) and -20% (1986). Y-axis labeled 'WHAT WHITE MALES AVERAGE' with ticks at -10 and -20.

documents.title: Post employees' responses on discrimination and advancement, by race/sex/job category
documents.subject: Typed compilation of Washington Post employees' first-person answers to an internal survey on race and sex discrimination, promotions, assignments, and recruiting at The Post
documents.date: approx mid-1990s (references the '94 race coverage and Matt Lewis as city editor; also cites 1982 and mid-50s)
documents.notes: Two-column typed page of quoted responses grouped under bold headings: 'White male, Photo:', 'Black male, Reporter:', 'White female, Metro, Reporter:', 'White male, section blank, Reporter:', 'White male, Style/News Desk/Sports/Editorial, Editor:', 'White female, Editor:', 'White female, Style/News Desk/Sports/Editorial/other, Reporter:'. Appears to be responses to a questionnaire (mentions 'Question 24'). Not a standard exhibit, memo, letter, or report format — classified as 'other'. Possibly related to DOC-001 as survey/Pay-equity background material, but it is a distinct document, so grouped separately.

pages.transcript:
[left column]

White male, Photo:

Question 24 raises an interesting point in my mind. I would like to see the rate of reporter separated from the issue he/she is covering. I think it was unfortunate that Milt Coleman was assigned to Jesse Jackson in the '94 race coverage. Perhaps this could be written off as coincidence or as Milton's preference (I'm not sure of his preference). If a reporter finds him/herself in a situation where his/her race would affect coverage (e.g. a black infiltrating where higher race allowances must be made, obviously, but in general I think assignments are sometimes unnecessarily tied to race.

Black male, Reporter:

The problem at The Post is not so much racism, in the sense of managers not wanting to see minorities promoted, as an inability of the managers to see potential in people who are unlike themselves. There is, in addition, a tendency on the part of top management to put too low a ceiling on minorities, that is to think primarily of white men when it comes to grooming people for higher-level jobs.

There has been a welcome trend in recent years of placing black reporters in jobs and/or sections of the paper that they used not to be considered for — National/Financial/Investigations/Foreign. Financial, etc. But there seems to be the sense in the newsroom that (Matt Lewis notwithstanding) city editor is about the top job any black reporter/editor should aspire to.

The Post frequently seems to interpret equal opportunity as meaning that if minorities and women work hard and follow directions, they too can become white men. I'm thinking particularly of (can I use a name?) Eddie Sargent, a nondirectional hire who, because of background, could bring us stories and insights into a segment of the city that we've never covered adequately. That was a gutsy idea. But Eddie is now floundering because his editors seem to see him as an inadequate suburban white man. For example, he could be bringing us important insights into the problems inner city youngsters face in school; some sense of how young black men cope (or fail to cope) in a middle-class town, or what tempts them into criminality. But we have him covering schools in the most traditional sort of way, a fact that magnifies his weaknesses and hides his potential strengths.

Patrice Gaines-Carter is another wasted opportunity. Instead of looking for ways to capitalize on her insights, sensitives and fine writing, the desk seems to be trying to turn her into just another suburban white reporter. Somebody should be working with her to develop ideas and assignments that allow us to take advantage of her special gifts.

I'm not really crazy about a special AME for minority staffers — a Purite Victorious "deputy for the colored" — but it might make sense for Ben or Len to have regular meetings with a small group of black staffers in order to get them a sense of where the trouble spots and squandered opportunities might be.

White female, Metro, Reporter:

All you have to do is look at The North Wall for the answer to question 1. The Post simply doesn't pay enough attention to all people's careers and the result is that white males, who started off with the advantage in the early 70s, stay ahead.

It does not train editors and does not make sure that blacks get the reporting background they need before moving ahead. The result is damaged careers and blacks leaving. In other cases, they are shunted aside and their knowledge of the city ignored by managers who think being a white male is an important criterion for excellence.

[right column]

A corporate culture prevails that continues to favor white males in everything from salaries to assignments and promotions — and the paper continues to hire more males from outside for managerial positions instead of promoting women and blacks who are here. Thus, the managerial pool remains white male. Readers are robbed of a diversity of judgments as to what is news — and people who work here continue to lose opportunities to advance. If someone is appointed to watch over careers, he or she should be charged with monitoring and helping everyone's career — perhaps with special emphasis on correcting discriminatory practices that harm blacks and women.

I do think The Post has made tremendous progress in helping parents to combine work and family, which has helped a number of women continue their careers after having babies — and kept them in the management pool.

White male, section blank, Reporter:

The root of the problem is a failure to cultivate black journalists at the high school and college levels. The Post, rather than inflating its ranks with unqualified blacks in order to meet a quota, should finance internships for blacks and school programs. The ranks of black journalists should be expanded, but not on a knee-jerk basis. Of course, the paper should also compete vigorously for qualified blacks in provincial areas, as well as make a greater effort to sponsor promising candidates from local universities such as Howard and UDC.

White male, Style/News Desk/Sports/Editorial, Editor:

This questionnaire does not address the most frightening form of discrimination at The Post — age discrimination. White males seem to systematically disappear from the newsroom sometime in their mid-50s. One would hope it is not because they are at an end, and that when the many younger women and blacks hired in recent years have put in their requisite years at The Post, they will share the burden of filling the apparent quota.

White female, Editor:

In a city with a large Hispanic population, why has The Post not made a greater effort to recruit Hispanic and Spanish-speaking reporters? Also Asians?

I suggest Post managers look to IBM where each manager is required to assist his subordinates in planning their careers and advancing within the organization. Here it seems managers are interested only in advancing their own careers, often at the expense of their subordinates.

I have applied for 25 jobs within The Post during the past three years and feel like I am pounding my head against the proverbial brick wall.

White female, Style/News Desk/Sports/Editorial/other, Reporter:

I think The Post should try to recruit more higher quality black editors and reporters and should not promote those who are at the not-top-notch quality just because they are black. The Style section sorely needs to cover black Washington better — both in quantity of stories and depth. Many stories about blacks are not developed fully throughout the entire paper, too.

documents.title: Draft letter to Ben Bradlee Jr. ('Len') on Post handling of Juan Williams sexual harassment complaints
documents.subject: Unsigned draft letter from Post employees (drafted by Martha Hamilton, Nell Henderson and others) to Len [Bradlee Jr.] expressing concern over management's handling of repeated sexual harassment complaints against Post writer Juan Williams and recommending changes to Post policy
documents.notes: Typed letter dated Nov. 1, 1991 with handwritten annotation at top: 'letter drafted by Martha Hamilton Nell Henderson and others'. Paper clip visible at top left. Page 2 (next image) is a badly rotated, mostly obscured photo whose visible text fragments ('...11 cases...', '...claim...', '...Carol...', '...ten Post,') plausibly belong to this letter's continuation/signature page, so it is grouped here with low page-level confidence; the match cannot be verified.

pages.transcript:
[handwritten at top] letter drafted by Martha Hamilton
Nell Henderson and others

Nov. 1, 1991

Dear Len,

We, the undersigned, want to express our continued concern over the way newsroom management has handled the repeated sexual harassment complaints by almost two dozen Post employees (male and female) over at least four years against Post writer Juan Williams.

Although we feel sympathy for Juan's family and understand the Post's policy of maintaining the confidentiality of personnel actions, we feel Juan's unrebuted [sic] false statements to the national media continue to cause anguish and professional harm to the women involved. They also have left many people inside and outside the Post with the impression that either the complaints were not serious or were not taken seriously. This continues to harm the Post as an institution and raises concerns for all of us who have a right to work in an environment free of discrimination and hostility.

This case illustrates the inadequacy of the Post's handling of sexual harassment complaints. The Post needs to take stronger steps to send a clear and unequivocal message to everyone here that such behavior will not be tolerated. We recommend that the Post's policy be improved in the following ways:

• The policy of confidentiality, while appropriate in most cases, is ill-suited in the case of an individual making false public comments that are injurious to his colleagues.

The Post has an obligation to set the record straight by refuting such comments. The Post could publicly state simply that its inquiry determined that the complaints were of substance, were substantiated and led to disciplinary action.

The Post need not publicly specify the complaints, the names of the complainants, or the action.

• When complaints are verified, the Post should ask the victims how the matter can be resolved in a way that will restore their sense of safety and comfort in the workplace.

• Management also owes the victims a clear statement on how the matter was resolved.

• Lower-level supervisors should pass such complaints up the chain-of-command, rather than allowing them to fester, as they did in this case, for four years before reaching the North Wall.

We appreciate your attention to our concerns and understand your reluctance to further publicize a matter that continues to hurt the Post and many of our colleagues. However we feel the best way to lay it to rest is to confront it openly and honestly.

[Photo rotated approximately 90 degrees; page mostly folded/obscured against a table surface with other sheets at the right edge. Only scattered end-of-line text fragments are legible:] [...11 cases;] [...of] [...claims] [...under] [...twice] [...open by] [...lowing] [...form that] [...claim] [...Carol] [...ten Post,] [remainder illegible]

documents.title: Summary of statistical analysis for Newspaper Guild (salary and merit pay data)
documents.subject: Cover memorandum explaining decisions made in preparing salary lists, salary breakdowns, and merit pay summaries enclosed for the Newspaper Guild's (arbitration-related) data request
documents.notes: Single typed page with handwritten annotation top right: 'YR-END 1991 DATA'. Explains methodological choices: summary line per employee, first dollar amount on first salary record, merit-pay variables based only on salary history records coded "14", single-year breakdowns only because only three years of salary histories were provided, merit pay averages include zero values.

pages.transcript:
[handwritten, top right] YR-END 1991 DATA

September 14, 1993

Summary of statistical analysis for Newspaper Guild

Enclosed please find the lists, salary breakdowns and merit pay summaries, reflecting our best efforts at interpreting the Guild's request. The following decisions were made:

I. For the lists, a summary line was printed for each employee, rather than following the multi-line format of the original printout.

The list in order of salaries uses the first dollar amount on the first record for each employee.

The variables which summarize merit pay reflect only salary history records coded "14".

The "ID" value on each record corresponds to the order of that employee's salary history records on the original printout.

II. The salary breakdowns also use the first dollar amount on the first record for each employee.

III. Again, the merit pay averages by race, sex and year are based only on those salary history records coded "14".

Please note that only single year breakdowns were calculated, because only three years of salary histories were provided.

Merit pay averages include zero values, as they appeared in the data.

documents.title: Grievance/statement narrative, page 10 (paragraphs 33-35: blocked Azerbaijan trip, denied merit raise, 1999 work)
documents.subject: First-person numbered statement (page 10 of at least 10) alleging assignment bias and a blocked reporting trip to Azerbaijan, a denied merit-pay recommendation, and describing 1999 reporting accomplishments
documents.date: 1999 or later (text covers events through October 1999; document itself undated)
documents.notes: Typed page numbered '- 10 -' at bottom, first-person numbered paragraphs continuing a statement (paragraph 33 references being stopped from an Azerbaijan trip by Dan Morgan and David Ottaway with approval of assignment editor David Ignatius; paragraph 34 a denied merit pay increase; paragraph 35 bylines and Sunday Business sections in 1999, quote from AME Jill Dutt's e-mail of October 12, 1999). Consistent with Martha Hamilton's own grievance/arbitration statement.

pages.transcript:
coverage, including the groundbreaking 1997 and Pulitzer prize nominated series: How Warm Will It Get? An evaluation that year described my writing as having "a nice touch."

33. In 1998, with Ignatius' approval, I had planned to travel to Azerbaijan to write about oil and gas exploration by U.S. companies in the region and their efforts to build a pipeline to transport oil and gas from the region. I also had arranged with Mobil Oil, which was a local company notorious for being uncooperative with the press, to talk to their people in Azerbaijan about exploration and development activities there. Before I could make the trip, however, I was stopped. I was told that Dan Morgan (on the National staff) and David Ottaway (on Investigative) were working on a major take-out about oil and gas exploration in the Caspian region. I was the Post's oil and energy reporter, but that seemed to make no difference. They had staked out the territory, and I could not go. Glenn Kessler, who was my assignment editor, and David Ignatius, AME Financial, both told me they protested. However, I was blocked from taking the trip and doing the story in the manner I had planned. I later wrote a story about oil and gas exploration in the region from D.C. that led the Sunday Business section on 4/26/1998. This was another instance of my being big-footed to make way for male colleagues -- in this case on a story that was clearly on my beat.

34. Near the end of his tenure as AME, probably in 1997 or early 1998, AME David Ignatius told me that he had recommended me for a merit pay increase, but that it had been denied. He did not say why.

35. In 1999, I had 107 bylines, five of them on the front page. I had returned to general assignment reporting because of new family problems. I edited a Sunday section on utility deregulation at AME Jill Dutt's request, and I conceptualized, reported and wrote a Sunday Business section devoted to the subject of financial planning for retirement in September, 1999. Jill expressed her pleasure about the handling of both sections. "You are already doing a lot, leading the coverage on two ambitious Sunday packages of which I am very proud," she wrote in an e-mail October 12, 1999.
